title: Apps for Caregivers Get a Dose of AI, but That Might Not Be Enough
gist: A survey of caregiver apps (Medisafe, Caring Village, Mejo, Briggzy, Citizen Health's Ari) as they add AI assistants for the 63 million US family caregivers. Experts warn the apps are not FDA-reviewed or HIPAA-protected, and that the burden of keeping data up to date falls on already overloaded caregivers, which limits adoption.

insights.claim: According to AARP, an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability in 2025, spending up to 27 hours a week on average.
insights.speaker: AARP
insights.so_what: A large, underserved market for care-coordination software and services.
insights.quote: an estimated 63 million Americans cared for adults or children with a medical condition or disability
insights.locator: We're not alone in our struggles.

insights.claim: The author says the US caregiver crisis, with caregivers suffering poor health, financial strain and isolation, is getting worse.
insights.speaker: Jaclyn Greenberg
insights.so_what: Growing demand may support both consumer apps and policy spending on caregiving.

insights.claim: Caring Village, founded in 2015, has added an AI assistant called Julia that answers caregiving questions, alongside its calendars, task assignment and care plans.
insights.speaker: Jaclyn Greenberg
insights.so_what: Older apps are adding chatbots on top of existing features, which suggests AI is becoming standard in the category.

insights.claim: Mejo charges $6 a month or $60 a year for premium shared journaling, and is looking at AI to suggest questions for medical appointments.
insights.speaker: Bret Koncak
insights.so_what: Low price points show limited willingness to pay in consumer caregiving software.

insights.claim: Mejo's cofounder argues that most caregiving happens between care visits rather than in interactions with the health system, and that this gap is the product opportunity.
insights.speaker: Bret Koncak
insights.so_what: Points to the home-care coordination layer as an untapped area outside EHR-centric health IT.
insights.quote: a lot of it is about what happens between care visits

insights.claim: Citizen Health, launched in 2024, gathers patients' medical records with consent, deidentifies and harmonizes them to understand diseases, and works with patient advocacy groups on drug-development research.
insights.speaker: Nasha Fitter
insights.so_what: The business model is the rare-disease data asset, which pharma R&D can use, not consumer subscriptions.

insights.claim: Citizen Health's Ari, a beta AI 'health teammate' used over text, reads medical records, patient portals and Google Calendar, spots medication-timing patterns, prepares for appointments, and helps with insurance and benefits. For now it serves only rare-disease patients.
insights.speaker: Jaclyn Greenberg
insights.so_what: Agentic AI on top of medical records is reaching consumers through niche, high-need groups first.

insights.claim: A Harvard bioethicist notes that most caregiving AI apps are not medical devices and have not been reviewed by the FDA, so their safety and efficacy rest on the company's word.
insights.speaker: I. Glenn Cohen
insights.so_what: These apps face little regulation today, which could change if harm occurs.

insights.claim: Health data that caregivers enter into these apps is usually not protected by HIPAA because it does not come from a covered entity, so users rely only on contractual promises that often absolve the companies.
insights.speaker: I. Glenn Cohen
insights.so_what: Consumer health-data monetization sits outside HIPAA, which is both an opportunity and a regulatory risk for app makers.

insights.claim: Cohen warns that the data collected may also cover parents and other caregivers, not just the person receiving care.
insights.speaker: I. Glenn Cohen
insights.so_what: Raises the privacy exposure beyond the patient.

insights.claim: A caregiving training CEO has seen many apps fail because they are tedious to maintain: physicians, nurses and discharge planners won't log in to update them, so the work falls back on the caregiver.
insights.speaker: Denise M. Brown
insights.so_what: Without integration with clinical workflows, retention suffers, and automating data entry is where the real value lies.

insights.claim: The author, herself a caregiver, concludes that the benefits depend on updating the app regularly.
insights.speaker: Jaclyn Greenberg
insights.so_what: Engagement friction is the core product risk in the category.

insights.claim: A National Council on Aging director says apps can help integrate care, but the broader caregiver crisis needs government, the private sector and families all involved.
insights.speaker: Nicole Howell
insights.so_what: Points to public policy and funding, not apps alone, as the main lever.
insights.quote: It has to be government. It has to be private.
